blocks.text: The AI Assets MCP Servers page in AI Security Admin Portal provides a centralized inventory of discovered Model Context Protocol (MCP) server instances so you can understand where MCP is present in your environment and assess the potential security exposure introduced by server capabilities (e.g., file system access, network access, code execution) and other risk indicators. At a high level, it shows each MCP instance’s resource name, where it was detected (resource types such as VMs or containers and the resource path), programming language, and an overall risk score and risk level. It also includes a governance-style status, e.g., Approved, Disapproved, or Pending Review.
MCP servers provide a standardized way to extend language models with real-world capabilities while keeping integrations consistent and reusable.
The AI Assets - MCP Servers Page provides the following benefits and enables you to:

blocks.item: Reduce one-off connector work by standardizing how tools, prompts, and resources are exposed to models.
Support deploying the same MCP server patterns across multiple AI applications and environments.
Make model-to-tool interactions more explicit (for example, defined tools/resources), which helps governance when properly inventoried and reviewed.
Reduce user risk by supporting governance of approved MCP servers and limiting unsafe or noncompliant integrations.

blocks.heading: About the AI Assets - MCP Servers Page

blocks.text: On the AI Assets MCP Servers page (AI Infrastructure > AI Assets - MCP Servers), you can do the following:

blocks.item: Filter by Business Units.
View metrics from the following perspectives:
MCP Servers by Risk: View the distribution of MCP servers' potential blast radius if the MCP server is compromised. Ratings are categorized as Critical, High, Medium, or Low.
MCP Serverss by Status: View the distribution of governance status of each MCP server, categorized as Sanctioned, Unsanctioned, or Pending.
MCP Servers by Type: View the distribution of the MCP server based on the deployment type.
Search for a specific MCP.
Click Export to export the data and download the report as an Excel file.
Show or hide columns.
Show or hide filters.
Apply filters
Environment: Returns data about the environment where the MCP server was discovered, eg. AWS, Azure, or GCP.
Regions: Returns MCP servers for the selected regions. You can exclude regions as required.
Accounts: Returns results from selected cloud accounts.
Type: Returns MCP servers based on whether they are remote or local.
Source: Returns data based on the source from which MCP servers originate, such as AWS Bedrock Agent.
Asset Risk: Returns results that match the selected filter criteria. Risk signals may include:
Execution capabilities
File deletion operations
Directory traversal
External network access
Credential storage/handling
Processing of sensitive data (for example, PII)
Risk Score: Returns data based on the overall severity rating that indicates how risky a specific MCP server is.
Status: Returns data based on the current status of the MCP server.
to view specific data.
View a list of MCP Servers which were discovered. For each MCP server you can view:
Name: The name of the MCP server. Click the MCP Server name to view additional details.
General Information: Information such as type, path, source, account ID, account name, organization ID, and region. Click More Details for a graphical view.

Risk Level: Indicates the potential blast radius if this MCP server is compromised. The rating is based on capabilities such as system command execution, file write or delete access, credential storage or access, and outbound (external) network calls. Critical means the server can execute commands, modify files, handle credentials, and contact external services. Low means the server is primarily read-only, with no system-level access.
Lifecycle: Timeline showing the stages an AI model goes through from discovery to deployment, monitoring, and updates, with timestamps for key milestones.
The detailed information page also displays the following tabs:
Graph View

A graph shows the connections between the MCP Server, its client, and associated components such as, tools, prompts, resources, code repository, dependencies, API calls, network connections, file systems, etc. Red warning icons indicate issues within specific components, providing users with a clear map for assessing and resolving vulnerabilities.

The graphs also include attack paths that show how the resource is compromised either through public exposure, malware, by an IAM entity (user, service, role) with access privileges, vulnerabilities, etc. This information helps you analyze the issues in detail and remediate them immediately.
You can click the nodes to view additional details of each entity.
Tools
Use this tab to view tools information:
Search by tool name.
View a list of tools which were discovered. For each tool, you can view:
Name: The name of the tool.
Description: A human-readable summary of what the tool does and why it exists.

Parameters: Structured inputs a user (or client) sends when invoking an MCP tool. They define what the tool needs to run and often determine its security impact (for example, which file, host, or URL it can touch).
File Access: Indicates whether the tool has file access or not.
Network Access: Indicates whether the tool has network access or not.
Code Execution: Indicates whether the tool can execute code or system commands

Process Access: Indicates if the tool can view, start, stop, signal, or attach to running processes (for example, enumerate processes, kill processes, read process info, or interact with process memory or output).
File Path: The file-system path(s) the tool can access or that the tool targets (often tied to traversal risk).
Prompts

Use this tab to view prompt information. In an MCP setup, prompts are the instructions provided to the model, and, indirectly, to tools, that shape behavior and outputs. They’re typically captured in two primary types:

MCP Prompts: Instruction text provided to an MCP-enabled model to guide how it should respond and how it should use MCP tools. It typically includes the system prompt (rules and guardrails for the session) and the user prompt (the user’s task request), and may also include additional context such as tool descriptions, parameters, and prior conversation.

System Prompts: Instructions that define the model’s role, boundaries, safety rules, and operating constraints (for example, what the assistant must/never do, tone, and tool-use rules). Applied across the session and generally not user-editable.

User Prompts: The end user’s request or question. It provides the task intent and context (for example, Summarize this incident report or Generate Terraform for this configuration). It can change every turn and is user-controlled.
Type: The type of server, i.e., Remote or Local.
Environment: Indicates where the asset was discovered, e.g., AWS, Azure, GCP, etc.
Source: Indicates the specific location or service where the AI model was discovered, stored, or hosted.
Asset Risk: Indicates the overall measure of how much security risk an MCP server introduces to the environment where it runs, based on what the server can do.
Risk Score: Indicates the overall severity rating that indicates how risky a specific MCP server is. Risk levels are classified as Critical, High, Medium, or Low,
Last Discovered: The timestamp of when the MCP server was discovered.
Status: The approval status of the MCP server, e.g., Pending, Sanctioned, or Unsanctioned.
